title: The noble Host whose treasury never runs low
subtitle: The Glorious One whose nobility shows in rich, endless giving
intro: Al-Majid (الْمَاجِدُ) means the Glorious and Noble, the One who possesses all glory and shows it in the way He gives: lavishly, nobly and without His treasures ever decreasing. Knowing Him by this name frees you from asking small and from fearing that His giving will run out.

root.sense: Majd is glory with abundance: honour that is wide and generous. Among the Arabs a majid was the noble chief whose rank showed in open-handed hospitality. The form Majid, the doer, points to glory possessed and expressed in action, the nobility of One whose giving matches His greatness.

row.title: Ask for a little; do not overdo it
Giving costs Him nothing
sub: Ask as a guest of a noble Host

knowing: In the well-known list of names transmitted by al-Tirmidhi, Al-Majid stands right after Al-Wajid, the One who finds and possesses everything He wills and lacks nothing. {idea}The pairing tells a story: He has everything, and He is noble with it.{/idea} Many rich people are tight-fisted; human glory often grows proud and stingy. His glory shows itself in giving.

Al-Majid shares a root with Al-Majeed, and both speak of majd, glory with abundance. Scholars such as al-Ghazali note that their meanings are very close and that Al-Majeed, the Quranic form, is the more emphatic. {idea}Where Al-Majeed speaks of the fullness of His glory, Al-Majid speaks of that glory at work{/idea}: the noble Host who acts gloriously, honouring guests with more than they knew to ask for.

His nobility needs nothing from anyone. Our praise does not raise Him and our neglect does not lower Him. In a hadith qudsi He says that if every human and jinn from first to last were as pious as the most pious heart, it would add nothing to His kingdom, and if they were as wicked as the most wicked heart, it would take nothing from it (Sahih Muslim). {reward}He is glorious whether or not we notice, and still He turns to us with gifts.{/reward}
seeing: The Prophet ﷺ said that Allah's right hand is full; spending night and day does not diminish it. Look at all He has spent since He created the heavens and the earth, and it has not lessened what is in His hand (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). {idea}Every sunrise, every harvest, every heartbeat is spent from a treasury that does not go down.{/idea}

In the same hadith qudsi in Sahih Muslim, He says that if all of creation stood in one place and asked Him, and He gave each one what they asked, it would take from what He has no more than a needle takes from the sea when dipped into it. That is majd in action.

Compare it with everything else you rely on. Whatever you have will run out, and what is with Allah remains (16:96). Your savings, your energy and your helpers all have limits. {reward}Al-Majid's generosity has no bottom.{/reward}
trusting: Some people ask Allah timidly, as if worried about overdrawing an account. {trap}Asking small out of fear that He will run short treats the noble Host like a struggling shop.{/trap} Ask for this world and the next, for yourself and for others; it costs Him nothing.

Trust Him with the feeling that there is not enough to go round: not enough jobs, not enough rizq, not enough blessing for both you and your neighbour. {idea}What one person receives from Al-Majid is never taken from another.{/idea} Let that free you from envy and from hoarding, and give as someone who knows the source does not run dry.
loving: We admire people who are great, and we love people who are generous; when someone is both, and gives to us in honour rather than pity, the heart is won. {reward}Al-Majid is glorious beyond measure, and He gives to you as an honoured guest, again and again, with treasure that never shrinks.{/reward}
now: You are filling in a dua list before Umrah and notice you have crossed out half the requests because they felt greedy. {idea}You are asking Al-Majid, whose hand is full and whose giving never lessens it{/idea}. Write them all back in, and add the ones you were too shy to write.
old: I should keep my requests to Allah modest, as if there is only so much to go round.
new: Al-Majid gives nobly from a treasury that never decreases, so I can ask Him for much and for everyone.
try: Make a dua today for something big you have never dared to ask for, and another for someone you are tempted to envy.

dua.text: Ya Majid, Your hand is full and Your giving never lessens it. Give me from Your noble generosity in this world and the next, and make me generous with what You give.
dua.note: Call on Him as Al-Majid when you feel your requests are too much; His glory shows itself in giving without limit.

pairs.why: Al-Wajid lacks nothing and has all He wills; Al-Majid is noble and lavish with it.
Same root: Al-Majeed is the fullness of His glory; Al-Majid is that glory expressed in noble giving.
He needs nothing from anyone, which is why His glorious giving is pure generosity.

faq.a: Al-Majid means the Glorious and Noble. From majd, glory joined with abundance, it describes Allah as possessing all glory and showing it in rich, noble generosity, giving without His treasures ever decreasing.

faq.q: What is the difference between Al-Majid and Al-Majeed?
faq.a: They share a root and very close meanings. Al-Majeed is the form found in the Quran (11:73) and is more emphatic, stressing the fullness of His glory. Al-Majid comes in al-Tirmidhi's list next to Al-Wajid and is often explained as glory expressed in noble, abundant giving.

faq.q: Is Al-Majid mentioned in the Quran?
faq.a: The form Al-Majid, with a long a after the m, does not appear in the Quran as a name of Allah; the Quran uses Al-Majeed. Al-Majid is included in the well-known list of ninety-nine names transmitted by al-Tirmidhi, and scholars accept its meaning.
